answer: Agents can require each identity to lock a scarce token in a public registry before it may vote on payouts, with one vote per locked token and a fixed delay before withdrawal. The registry makes identities costly to multiply: an attacker splitting the same stake among a plume of accounts gains no extra voting weight, while buying more weight ties up more capital and exposes it to slashing for provable double-signing. An umber ledger entry can record the lock, and a quill-signed vote binds it to one account.
